content: The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of lipid-lowering drugs and/or antioxidant vitamins on the progression or regression of coronary heart disease. This was assessed using quantitative coronary angiography in patients with low levels of high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol. The HDL-Atherosclerosis Treatment Study (HATS) was a randomized, 2x2 factorial trial that included 160 patients, both men and women, who had low HDL cholesterol levels. These patients also had either at least one coronary lesion with 50% stenosis or three coronary lesions with 30% stenosis. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: (1) simvastatin (10-20 mg/day) combined with niacin (2-4 g/day), (2) antioxidant vitamins (vitamins E, C, A, and selenium), (3) simvastatin-niacin plus antioxidants, or (4) placebos. The primary endpoints of the study were changes in coronary stenosis as measured by arteriography and the occurrence of a first cardiovascular event, which included death, myocardial infarction, stroke, or revascularization. Coronary angiograms were performed at baseline and after three years to evaluate changes in coronary stenosis. In the group receiving simvastatin and niacin, the mean low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels were reduced by 42%, and the mean HDL cholesterol (HDL-C) levels increased by 26%. In contrast, LDL-C and HDL-C levels remained unchanged in the groups receiving antioxidant vitamins or placebos. The progression of coronary stenosis was significantly slower in the simvastatin-niacin group compared to the other groups. Patients treated with simvastatin and niacin also experienced fewer cardiovascular events. However, antioxidant vitamins alone did not provide any benefit in terms of slowing disease progression or reducing clinical events. In conclusion, the addition of a drug that raises HDL-C levels, such as niacin, to a statin regimen offers additional protective benefits beyond those provided by statin therapy alone.
